pages.x: After Napoleon, Italy was again split into small states, with Austria ruling Lombardy and Venice and the pope ruling the middle. Giuseppe Mazzini, a revolutionary from Genoa, founded Young Italy in 1831 to make one free republic of it all. His risings failed again and again, but his idea spread.

In 1848 Milan threw out the Austrians in five days of street fighting, and Venice and Rome declared themselves republics. King Charles Albert of Piedmont-Sardinia went to war with Austria and was beaten. In 1849 French troops crushed the Roman Republic, which Garibaldi had defended, and the Austrians came back.

Cavour, prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia from 1852, built railways, sent troops to the Crimean War to win friends, and secretly agreed with Napoleon III of France to drive Austria out together. In 1859 they won bloody battles at Magenta and Solferino, and Piedmont gained Lombardy. Tuscany and its neighbours soon voted to join.

A Swiss businessman, Henry Dunant, reached Solferino the evening after the battle and found some 40,000 dead and wounded lying in the heat with hardly any care. He got local women to nurse men of both sides, and later wrote a book about it. It led to the founding of the Red Cross in 1863 and the first Geneva Convention.

A chorus from Giuseppe Verdi's opera Nabucco of 1842, in which Hebrew slaves long for their lost homeland, came to stand for Italy's own longing. Walls were painted with VIVA VERDI, which also spelled out Viva Vittorio Emanuele Re D'Italia: long live Victor Emmanuel, King of Italy.

In May 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi, a sailor turned soldier who had fought for freedom in South America, sailed from near Genoa with about a thousand volunteers in red shirts. They landed at Marsala in Sicily, beat the much bigger army of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, crossed to the mainland and took Naples.

Cavour feared Garibaldi would march on Rome and drag France into the war, so Piedmont's army marched south through the pope's lands. In October 1860 Garibaldi met King Victor Emmanuel II near Teano, greeted him as king of Italy and handed over his conquests. Then he went home to his farm on the island of Caprera.

The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in March 1861, and Cavour died weeks later. Venice was won in 1866, when Italy sided with Prussia against Austria. Rome, guarded by French troops, came last: when France called them home to fight Prussia in 1870, Italian soldiers broke through the walls at Porta Pia, and Rome became the capital. The pope called himself a prisoner in the Vatican.

Italy was made in a dozen years, more by war and diplomacy than by the will of its people: most Italians still spoke their own dialects. As one statesman put it, Italy had been made, and now Italians had to be made. The gap between the richer north and the poorer south is still felt today.
